evidence.label: A Counterexample to Kurosh’s Division-Ring Problem

headline: A division ring made from two elements, each element algebraic, can still be infinite-dimensional over its center.
scope: The example is one countable division ring of characteristic zero. The degree of the polynomial each element satisfies is allowed to grow without bound.
plain: A division ring is a number system where you can divide by anything nonzero, but multiplication need not commute. Kurosh asked in 1941 about such rings generated by finitely many elements, where every element solves a polynomial equation. Must they be finite in size over their center? This paper claims not. It builds a two-generated ring where every element solves some polynomial, yet the ring is infinite-dimensional over its center.
doesNot: This does not give a ring where one polynomial degree works for every element; that case was already known to force finite size.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it answers a question Kurosh posed in 1941, which positive results had settled only under extra hypotheses.

explanation:
Start with the quaternions, numbers like q = 1 + 2i + 3j. Here i² = j² = −1, and ij = −ji, so order matters. Square q. The cross terms 6ij and 6ji cancel, and q² = −12 + 4i + 6j. Then q² − 2q = −14. So q solves the equation q² − 2q + 14 = 0, whose coefficients are ordinary real numbers.

Every quaternion solves such an equation. The 2 is twice the real part, and the 14 is 1 + 4 + 9. The real numbers are the center of the quaternions: the numbers that commute with everything. A ring is algebraic over its center when every element solves a nonzero polynomial with central coefficients. The quaternions are also small: every quaternion is built from 1, i, j and ij, so they have dimension 4 over the reals.

A division ring is a number system where every nonzero element can be divided by, though multiplication need not commute. The Kurosh problem asks whether algebraic over the center forces local finiteness[1]. Locally finite means anything generated by finitely many elements has finite dimension over the center. Alexander Kurosh asked this in 1941, inspired by Burnside's problem about groups[5].

Positive results came under extra conditions. If one degree bound works for every element, the ring satisfies a polynomial identity, and theorems of Jacobson and Kaplansky then give local finiteness[7]. Bell, Drensky and Sharifi sharpened this to dimension at most d² over the center[8]. Golod built infinite-dimensional algebras of a related kind in 1964. But they contain nonzero elements whose powers vanish, so they are not division rings[6].

This paper gives a negative answer[2]. It builds a countable division ring of characteristic zero, generated over its center by two elements x and y[3]. Every element is algebraic over the center, yet the ring has infinite dimension over it[3]. The trick is that each element may need its own polynomial, of growing degree[4]. That is exactly what the uniform-degree results forbid.

The construction is a long iteration. Countability matters here: it lets the paper list every polynomial expression in x and y and treat them one at a time[10]. At each stage a lifting theorem makes the next listed expression algebraic over a larger central field[11]. The same step enlarges the division algebra and keeps every earlier equation true[12]. A limiting construction, called an ultraproduct, then keeps all these equations at once[13].

The one obstacle is keeping the process alive. Each step must leave two independent directions free and keep x and y generating everything[11]. Otherwise the next step would have nothing to work with. Most of the paper proves that these properties survive every step, using matrix calculations and formal power series. A last argument shows the dimension is infinite over the true center, which the construction does not fix in advance[14].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper. The claim rests on the paper's own long argument. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. No Lean check is listed and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A number system where every nonzero element can be divided by; multiplication need not commute.
The elements of a ring that commute with every other element.
Every element solves some nonzero polynomial equation with coefficients from the center.
Anything generated by finitely many elements has finite dimension over the center.
A fixed polynomial equation that holds for all choices of elements in the ring.
